title: The water-path detectives
subtitle: Summer 1 • Trace movement and respect the evidence
objective: Explain the root–stem–leaf water pathway and use dye evidence to identify internal transport in a cut shoot.

sow.exactOutcome: Explain how water travels through a plant.
sow.alignment: Chronological continuation of the supplied SOW. This lesson develops or reviews the named outcome; it does not claim an accreditation award.

success: Trace soil water through roots and stem to leaves.
Explain what coloured internal pathways support.
State a limit of a rootless demonstration.

vocabulary.meaning: Movement of a substance from one place to another.
Plant pathways that carry water and dissolved minerals.
A marker used to help follow movement.

equipment: Printed shared evidence and one chosen pupil route; pencil; optional ruler; projector or offline HTML.
Optional adult-prepared cut white-flower shoots, stable plastic cups, dilute food colouring, plain-water comparison and tray; prepared stem sections.
preparation: Print the shared evidence, one response route and exit page. Routes are alternatives, not a workload ladder.
Read the worked answers. Prepare an oral, pointing or adult-scribed route where useful.

Prepare any coloured-water shoots and plain-water comparison well before the lesson; real staining may take hours or longer and can vary. The supplied constructed observations allow full teaching without waiting.

Only an adult cuts stems or sections using the school’s usual safe method, outside pupil handling. Keep a comparison in plain water and prepare labelled observation cards. A cut celery stalk is a leaf stalk, not a complete stem; this pack uses a cut flower stem.
safety: Use adult-selected non-toxic plant material and small amounts of dilute food colouring; nothing is eaten or drunk.
Adults prepare all cuts; pupils do not use blades. Cover surfaces, use stable cups in trays, wipe spills and wash hands.
Keep liquids away from electrical devices. No pressurised or heated apparatus is needed.
practicalAlternative: All core reasoning uses the supplied evidence and can be completed in 40 minutes without a live practical.

misconceptions.claim: Water mainly travels up the outside of the stem.
misconceptions.correction: The dye comparison can reveal internal water-carrying pathways.
misconceptions.check: Ask where the adult-cut section shows colour.

misconceptions.claim: A cut shoot proves how roots absorb water.
misconceptions.correction: The cut shoot has no roots; it gives evidence about transport above the cut.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether roots are present in the setup.

misconceptions.claim: Any falling water level proves every lost drop entered the plant.
misconceptions.correction: Water can also evaporate from a container.
misconceptions.check: Compare a cup without a plant.

access.supported: Short choices, word bank and pointing or adult-scribed reasons; same core scientific goal.
access.standard: Make a short evidence-based explanation or record using the supplied information.
access.stretch: Apply the core idea to a changed case, evaluate evidence or identify a limit.
access.regulation: Preview the sequence. Offer seated observation, quiet paired rehearsal, private feedback and a pass from public sharing. Routes respond to current access needs, not a diagnosis.

sources.title: Science and Plants for Schools: water transport
sources.note: Checked 8 September 2026. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals; evaporation from leaves contributes to pulling water upwards. Phloem sugar transport is distinct.

sources.title: Science and Plants for Schools: how does water travel through a plant?
sources.note: Checked 8 September 2026. Dye evidence can reveal internal water pathways. Our cut-shoot demonstration is explicitly not a complete rooted plant.

slides.title: How can water reach a leaf above the soil?
body: Use a marker to test part of it.
slides.notes: Distinguish the rooted-plant explanation from the rootless demonstration. Neither pupils nor the lesson need to wait for colour to develop.

slides.title: Retrieve the connected parts
body: 1. Which part takes in soil water?
2. Which part connects roots and leaves?
3. Does water usually enter as solid soil?
slides.notes: 1 roots. 2 stem. 3 no; roots absorb water and dissolved mineral nutrients, not chunks of soil.

slides.title: I trace the rooted-plant route
slides.notes: Think aloud: “I begin with water in soil, enter a root and follow xylem through the stem to a leaf. Some water evaporates and leaves as vapour.” Evaporation from leaves helps pull water upward; a straw-sucking mouth is not the mechanism.

visual.title: Water travels through internal pathways
visual.description: Selected water path in a rooted plant: soil water enters roots, travels upward in xylem through the stem, reaches leaves, and some leaves as water vapour. Arrows do not imply that all absorbed water is lost or that root uptake was demonstrated by a cut shoot.

elements.text:
Water travels up
inside the stem
to leaves.

Some water leaves
the leaves as vapour.
These water-carrying pathways are called xylem.

slides.title: I mark water in a cut shoot
body: A plain-water shoot is the comparison.
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “I can investigate movement in this shoot, but I cannot claim to have shown root uptake because there are no roots.” Food colouring marks some pathways; it is not normal plant food.

visual.title: Follow a visible tracer
visual.description: Two cut flower shoots stand in separate cups, one with coloured water and one with plain water. Dye can mark internal water routes in the shoot; neither shoot has roots. The plain-water cup is a comparison.

elements.text: Cut shoots: this demonstration has no roots.

slides.title: I inspect the interior evidence
body: Not all tissue is coloured equally.
slides.notes: Shares I do time. Think aloud: “Inside colour supports transport through internal pathways. A coloured outer surface alone would be weaker evidence.” Xylem name is helpful but not required for supported core explanation.

visual.title: Inspect inside, not just outside
visual.description: Simplified adult-prepared stem cross-sections from the dye and plain-water comparison. Coloured spots represent selected stained water-carrying bundles, not uniform colouring of every tissue. Positions are illustrative and not a precise anatomy atlas.

slides.title: Sequence the evidence before explaining
slides.notes: W1: B then C then D. Use evidence reader, sequencer and sceptic roles. Ask what the plain-water comparison adds: colour comes from the dye condition. Records are constructed; no universal 2-hour or 24-hour rate is implied.

rows: Internal red paths; then some red petals
table.caption: Constructed observations; timings vary in real demonstrations

slides.title: Which claim reaches too far?
body: “We proved how roots took up water.”
slides.notes: W2: first supported; second unsupported because no roots. F also blocks “every missing drop entered the shoot”, because evaporation can reduce water level.
slides.reveal: Explain the demonstrated part of the route and state what was not tested.

slides.title: What does an internal red path support?
body: Focus on evidence inside the shoot.
slides.notes: Correct first option. Revisit the section diagram if pupils treat the entire stem as one hollow pipe.

options.text: Coloured water moved through internal pathways.
options.feedback: The tracer appears within the cut section.

options.text: The demonstration directly observed root absorption.
options.feedback: There are no roots in this setup.

options.text: The dye is the plant’s natural food.
options.feedback: It is a tracer; green plants make their own sugars.

slides.title: Choose your science route
slides.notes: Set ONE route. Require a connected route and a claim limited to the evidence. A diagram with correctly directed arrows can replace prose. Do not require detailed transpiration physics or a perfect anatomical section.

slides.title: Make your own evidence record
slides.notes: Require a connected route and a claim limited to the evidence. A diagram with correctly directed arrows can replace prose. Do not require detailed transpiration physics or a perfect anatomical section.

slides.title: Check what the evidence can show
body: Point to the clue you used.
slides.notes: Shares independent time. Ask for a reason, not just a correct word. Require a connected route and a claim limited to the evidence. A diagram with correctly directed arrows can replace prose. Do not require detailed transpiration physics or a perfect anatomical section.

slides.title: Lundy loop: improve the shared account
slides.notes: Listen to a selected pupil revision and visibly adopt a scientifically accurate contribution. Offer private, written or partner feedback.
slides.prompt: Which limit made the explanation more trustworthy?
slides.reveal: The rootless shoot supports internal transport, while the full root pathway is a separate scientific model.

slides.title: Keep the useful change
slides.notes: Shares review time. Name how a pupil contribution changed a label, method or conclusion. Do not rank pupils.
slides.reveal: The rootless shoot supports internal transport, while the full root pathway is a separate scientific model.

slides.title: Three final checks
body: E1. Which part takes in water from soil?
E2. Does water travel through internal stem pathways?
E3. Did the cut-shoot experiment contain roots?
slides.notes: Collect brief individual evidence. Use the answer key and re-teach the specified misconception if needed.

pupilPages.title: Shared evidence • The water-path case file
pupilPages.intro: Records C–F are constructed teaching observations. Real dye timing varies; use the evidence supplied today.

cards.title: A • Rooted-plant model
cards.text: Soil water enters roots, then travels inside the stem to leaves. Some water leaves as vapour.

cards.title: B • Setup
cards.text: Two similar cut white-flower shoots: one in red-coloured water, one in plain water. Neither has roots.

cards.title: C • After 2 hours
cards.text: Constructed observation: red lines appear inside the dye shoot’s adult-cut stem section.

cards.title: D • After 24 hours
cards.text: Constructed observation: some petals show red colour. Exact timing varies in real plants.

cards.title: E • Plain-water comparison
cards.text: Constructed observation: no red dye colour in the control stem or petals.

cards.title: F • Water-level check
cards.text: A separate open cup without a plant also loses some water. Evaporation is possible.

blocks.prompt: W1. Put setup, internal colour and petal colour in order.
W2. Which part of the full rooted-plant route was not tested by B?

pupilPages.title: Route 1 • Build the water route
pupilPages.intro: Word bank: soil / roots / stem / leaves / inside.

blocks.prompt: S1. Complete the route: soil → ___ → ___ → leaves.
S2. The red paths in C are...
S3. What was different about the water in the comparison shoot?
S4. Did the cut shoots have roots?
S5. State one thing the dye evidence supports.

pupilPages.title: Route 2 • Write a detective explanation
pupilPages.intro: Use the observation and explain what it supports.

blocks.prompt: M1. Draw or describe the full water route in a rooted plant.
M2. Explain how C and D support transport in the cut shoot.
M3. Explain why E is a useful comparison.
M4. State one thing B did not test and one reason F matters.

pupilPages.title: Route 3 • Challenge the overclaim
pupilPages.intro: A report says: “All water travelled up the outside. We proved root uptake, and every drop missing from the cup entered the plant.”

blocks.prompt: T1. Use C to challenge the outside-only claim.
T2. Use B to explain why direct root-uptake proof is missing.
T3. Use F to explain an alternative cause of water loss.
T4. Write a careful two-sentence conclusion that keeps the useful evidence.

pupilPages.title: Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Point, draw, write or tell an adult.

blocks.prompt: E1. Which part takes in water from soil?
E2. Does water travel through internal stem pathways?
E3. Did the cut-shoot experiment contain roots?
R1. Which idea did you improve or defend? What evidence helped?
R2. What useful question would you investigate next?

answers.label: Retrieval 1–3
answers.answer: 1 roots. 2 stem. 3 no; water with dissolved minerals is absorbed.

answers.label: We do W1–W2
answers.answer: W1 B setup, C internal stem colour, D later petal colour. E provides a plain-water comparison. W2 root uptake was not directly tested; no roots present. F shows evaporation as another cause of lost water.

answers.label: Hinge
answers.answer: First option correct. Internal tracer supports internal movement; no roots were present; dye is not natural plant food.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 roots, stem. S2 inside. S3 plain water without red dye. S4 no. S5 coloured water moved through internal pathways towards upper parts.

answers.label: M1–M4
answers.answer: M1 soil → roots → stem/xylem → leaves, with some water exiting as vapour if added. M2 tracer inside stem and later petals supports movement within the shoot to upper parts. M3 no red dye appears without the dye condition, helping distinguish tracer staining from a pre-existing colour. M4 roots were absent, so direct root uptake was not observed; F shows open water can evaporate without a plant.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 inside staining contradicts outside-only movement. T2 the shoots were cut and rootless. T3 evaporation from the exposed water surface. T4 e.g. the coloured water produced internal stained paths and later petal colour, supporting movement through this cut shoot. It did not directly test root uptake or show that every drop lost from the cup entered the plant.

answers.label: Exit E1–E3
answers.answer: E1 roots. E2 yes, through xylem pathways. E3 no.

answers.label: R1–R2
answers.answer: Responses vary. Credit a scientific revision, evidence-based defence or relevant next question. A private or oral response has equal value.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2, retrieval 3, I do 7, We do 8, hinge 3, independent 12, review 3, exit 2. Zero-minute slides share the named stage time.
BUILD uses the supplied Year 3 science anchor with age-respectful contexts for older pupils. Supported, standard and stretch are selectable routes within the pathway.

Interactive We do: predict first, test against the controlled SVG model or supplied evidence, then explain or revise. Shared W tasks offer the equivalent paper discussion. Animation is a teaching representation, not filmed experimental evidence.
Keep constructed evidence separate from actual class observations. Do not invent measurements or require internet research.
Secure core: roots → stem → leaves with internal transport, plus recognition that the demonstration lacks roots. Re-teach the limit by physically pointing to what is and is not in the apparatus.

interactive.title: Trace, test and limit the water claim
interactive.intro: Use the rooted model and constructed cut-shoot records. Reveal each diagram after a prediction; timings are not a live experiment.
